links.note: In 90 the anicham is the measure of fragility: it wilts when merely smelled (மோப்பக் குழையும்), and a guest wilts at a changed face. In 1111 the man grants the flower that same good nature (நன்னீரை) and then says the woman he loves is softer still (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்). The book's standard of delicacy in the ethics of hospitality becomes the thing a lover's praise has to exceed.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham (நின்னினும் மென்னீரள்); 1289 says love itself is more delicate than a flower (மலரினும் மெல்லிது காமம்) and few catch its right moment. The same comparative, softer than a flower, is applied first to the beloved's body and later to the experience of love.

In 1112 the man scolds his heart for being confused by flowers, as if her eyes were like blossoms that many can see (பலர்காணும் பூ); Parimelazhagar takes the point to be that her eyes are seen by him alone. 1119 turns the same phrase on the moon: to match her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). Both rest on one criterion: what is open to everyone's gaze cannot equal what is his alone.

1113 lists her features as metaphors: body a tender shoot (முறி), teeth pearls, and kohl-lined eyes that are spears (வேலுண்கண்). 1084 had already noticed the mismatch this list contains: her eyes, with a look that eats the life of those who see them, are at war (அமர்த்தன) with her gentle womanly nature. Read together, the spear in the inventory of soft things is the same contradiction 1084 names outright.

1113 praises her as bamboo-shouldered (வேய்த்தோளவட்கு). 906, in the chapter on men ruled by their wives, says those who fear the wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no standing even if they live like the gods. The same stock epithet of beauty is admired in the Book of Love and named in the Book of Wealth as the thing an unmanned husband fears.

In 1094 the woman, when he looks at her, looks at the ground (நிலன்நோக்கும்). In 1114 the blue lilies, if they could see her, would bow and look at the ground (கவிழ்ந்து நிலன்நோக்கும்), admitting they cannot match her eyes. The flowers are given her own gesture of shyness, here as shame at being outdone.

1114 imagines lilies hanging their heads because they cannot equal her eyes (கண்ணொவ்வேம்). In 1231, during separation, the friend tells her that her eyes are now ashamed before fragrant flowers (நறுமலர் நாணின கண்); Parimelazhagar explains that weeping has dimmed them. The shame has changed sides: the superiority claimed in praise lasts only while the lovers are together.

475 warns that even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle if the load is piled too high (அச்சிறும்). 1115 says she has worn anicham flowers without removing the stalks (கால்களையாள்), so no good drums will sound for her waist; Parimelazhagar explains that the waist will break under the weight and get the funeral drum. Both make the lightest possible load the breaking one, as counsel on overreach in 475 and as playful hyperbole about her slenderness in 1115.

1111 says she is more delicate than the anicham. 1115 pushes the claim to a comic limit: the unremoved stalks of that same flower (அனிச்சப்பூக் கால்களையாள்) are too heavy for her waist. The flower that was the standard of softness becomes a burden.

In 1081 the man, at first sight, cannot tell whether she is a goddess, a peahen or a woman, and his heart reels (மாலும் என் நெஞ்சு). In 1116 the confusion is moved to the sky: the stars cannot tell the moon from her face (அறியா) and wander from their places (பதியின் கலங்கிய). The lover's own bewilderment about what she is becomes, in the praise chapter, a bewilderment he attributes to the stars.

1116 says the stars cannot distinguish the moon from her face. 1117 immediately denies that the two are alike: the moon fills out from loss and has a spot, and her face has none (மறுவுண்டோ). Parimelazhagar reads 1117 as mocking the stars for missing an obvious difference, so the second verse withdraws the equality the first seemed to grant.

957 says a fault in the well-born shows up high and clear like the spot on the moon in the sky (மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல்). 1117 asks whether her face has any spot as the bright moon has (மறுவுண்டோ மாதர் முகத்து). The moon's mark is the book's figure for the one visible flaw in something eminent, and the lover uses it to claim she has no such flaw.

782 uses the moon's phases for friendship: with the wise it fills like the crescent, with fools it shrinks like the moon after full. 1117 mentions the same cycle, a moon that shines only after filling its lost parts (அறுவாய் நிறைந்த), as a defect that her face does not share. The waxing that is a hopeful figure in 782 counts in 1117 as evidence of the moon's inconstancy.

Both verses address the moon with வாழி மதி. In 1118 the man tells it that it could have his love if it could shine like her face; Parimelazhagar hears the blessing as mockery. In 1210 the woman, left behind, asks it not to set so that her eyes may find the man who has gone without leaving her heart. The moon is a rival to be dismissed in the time of union and a helper to be begged in separation.

In 1119 the man tells the moon that to resemble her face it must not appear for many to see (பலர்காணத் தோன்றல்). In 1311 the woman refuses the man's chest because all women feast on him in common with their eyes (கண்ணின் பொதுஉண்பர்). Each lover applies the same standard from the other side: what is shared with every onlooker is no longer one's own.

1111 opens the chapter by ranking her above the anicham in softness. 1120 closes it by making the anicham and swan's down hurt her feet like the nerunji fruit, a thorn (மாதர் அடிக்கு நெருஞ்சிப் பழம்). The flower moves from being less soft than she is to being painful to her. Parimelazhagar sets the verse in a refusal to take her on a desert elopement.

64 says the gruel one's children have stirred with their small hands is far sweeter than amrita (அமிழ்தினும் ஆற்ற இனிது). 1121 says the moisture at her white teeth is like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன்கலந் தற்று). In both, affection makes something bodily and ordinary taste better than the finest food, for a parent in one verse and a lover in the other.

1121 calls her பணிமொழி, the woman of soft, low speech, in a verse about the sweetness of her kiss. In 1258 the woman uses the same word for his speech: the soft words (பணிமொழி) of that thief of many deceits are the weapon that breaks her womanly reserve. The quality he savours in her is the one she names in him as a weapon.

Both verses use the phrase உடம்பொடு உயிரிடை நட்பு, the friendship between body and life. In 1122 the man offers it as the model of closeness for his bond with her. In 338, in the chapter on impermanence, that same friendship is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell (குடம்பை) behind. Read with 338, the lover's comparison describes a bond that is intimate and also certain to end, which fits Parimelazhagar's heading for 1122 as spoken in fear of parting.

73 says the tie of the precious life to the body (என்போடு இயைந்த தொடர்பு) is itself said to be the way of being joined with love. 1122 says the tie between the man and the woman is what the tie of body and life is. One verse explains embodiment by love and the other explains a love by embodiment, so the two comparisons run in opposite directions and support each other.

In 1122 the man claims they are as body and life. In 1209 the woman says her life is ending as she thinks about the lack of kindness in the one who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்). Her line remembers a claim of exactly this kind and sets it against his absence; these are speeches in a drama, so this is her complaint in the moment, not a refutation.

In 1123 the man orders the image in the pupil of his eye (கருமணியிற் பாவாய்) to leave, since otherwise there is no room for the woman he loves. In 1126 the woman says her lover never leaves her eyes (கண்ணுள்ளின் போகார்) and is too subtle to be hurt when she blinks. Both lovers place the other inside the eye; he has to make room for her, and she has him there already.

1122 says their bond is like that of body and life. 1124 draws the consequence: together she is to his life what living is (வாழ்தல்), and when she leaves she is what dying is (சாதல்). The comparison in 1122 becomes a statement of what separation will mean.

In 1124 the man says her leaving is death to his life (சாதல் அதற்கன்னள் நீங்கும் இடத்து). In 1151 the reply to his announced journey is that news of his quick return should be told to those who will be alive then (வாழ்வார்க் குரை); Parimelazhagar gives the line to her friend, Manakkudavar to the woman. Each side says that separation is not survivable, he at a brief parting after a meeting and her side when he leaves on a long journey.

In 1125 the man says he would recall her qualities if he forgot them, but he does not know forgetting (மறப்பறியேன்). In 1207 the woman uses the same word, மறப்பறியேன், and asks what would become of her if she did forget, since even remembering burns her heart. Both deny that forgetting is possible; his version is a neat reply to her friend, and hers records what unbroken memory costs.

In 1125 the man avoids saying 'I remembered her', because remembering implies having forgotten (உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் மறப்பின்). In 1316 he says exactly that, 'I thought of you' (உள்ளினேன் என்றேன்), and she asks 'why did you forget?' (என்மறந்தீர்) and sulks. The later scene plays out the trap that the reply in 1125 was built to avoid.

In 1126 she says her lover does not leave her eyes and is not hurt even if she blinks (இமைப்பின் பருவரார்), because he is so subtle. In 1129 she will not blink, knowing he would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). The same conceit is used both ways within one chapter: blinking is harmless in the first verse and a risk in the second, which shows these are playful defences of him and not one consistent picture.

1126 says he never leaves her eyes though the town thinks him gone. 1218 says that when she sleeps he is on her shoulder and when she wakes he hurries into her heart (நெஞ்சத்தர் ஆவர் விரைந்து). Parimelazhagar frames both as her defence of him against the charge of absence: she answers by locating him somewhere inside herself at every moment.

Both verses turn on the moment of lining the eye with kohl. In 1127 she does not line her eyes at all (கண்ணும் எழுதேம்), because for that moment the lover who lives in them would be hidden. In 1285 the eye cannot see the stick while it is being lined (எழுதுங்கால் கோல்காணாக் கண்), and likewise she cannot see her husband's fault when she sees him. The same small blindness is something to avoid in one verse and the figure for love's blindness in the other.

1128 says that since her lover is in her heart (நெஞ்சத்தார் காதலவராக) she fears eating anything hot, knowing it would burn him. 1249 uses almost the same opening, உள்ளத்தார் காதலவராக, to ask her heart whom it goes out looking for when he is within it. The playful premise of 1128, said to defend him, is used in 1249 to rebuke her own restless heart.

In 1128 his presence in her heart is something she protects, to the point of avoiding hot food. In 1205 the same presence is a complaint: he keeps her out of his own heart and yet is not ashamed to come into hers without pause (எம்நெஞ்சத்து ஓவா வரல்). The later verse adds what 1128 leaves out, the question whether the dwelling is mutual.

In 1129 she does not blink for fear of losing sight of him, and for this the town calls him a stranger without love (ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர்). In 1220 the people of the town say he has left her in waking life, and she asks whether they do not see him in dreams (கனவினால் காணார்கொல்). In both she sets the town's outward evidence against her inner experience of his presence, first in the eye and then in the dream.

1129 and 1130 end with the same line, ஏதிலர் என்னும் இவ் வூர். 1129 gives the town's ground for blame, her sleeplessness, which she explains as refusing to blink. 1130 states her answer directly: he lives gladly in her heart always (உவந்துறைவர் உள்ளத்துள் என்றும்), while the town says he lives apart.

In 1130 she is sure that he lives in her heart, and gladly (உவந்துறைவர்), against the town's talk. In 1204 she affirms the same thing, that he is always in her heart (எந்நெஞ்சத்து ஓஒ உளரே அவர்), and then asks whether she too has a place in his (யாமும் உளேங்கொல் அவர்நெஞ்சத்து). The confidence she shows the town in 1130 does not answer the doubt she admits in 1204: his presence in her heart says nothing about her place in his.
